title: Chapter 64: The Ashborn, Part 4 of 5: The Putting-Back Page
html:
The tent they gave them was at the north edge of the camp, the last one before the ridge.
It was small and round and low, so low that Oren had to go in on his hands and knees and could not stand up inside at all, only sit hunched with his head bent under the hide roof. The frame was bent thorn wood, lashed together with sinew. The floor was gravel, covered with mats of woven grass, and over the mats there were furs. Goat skins, thick and shaggy and smelling strongly of goat. In the middle of the floor there was a ring of small stones with a few red coals in it, and over the coals there was the smoke hole, a round patch of dark sky with three stars in it.
On the outside of the tent there were handprints. Corin had seen them as they came in. Only a few. Six or seven, faded almost to nothing. Somebody had lived in this tent once and carried a few, and then had gone away, or died, and nobody had lived in it since.
Arran had brought them an oil lamp. A little clay one, like a shallow dish with a lip, with a twist of wool for a wick, burning goat fat. It gave a small yellow light and a thick smell. He had put it down on a flat stone by the fire ring, and grinned at them, and backed out of the door flap, and gone.
And before he went he had turned them round.
He had not said anything. He had only taken the furs, which Oren had laid out along the south wall of the tent, and moved them, one by one, without asking, to the north wall. So that when they lay down they would lie with their feet to the door and their faces to the ridge. Then he had looked at them, and nodded, and gone.
Now the three of them sat in the little round tent with the lamp between them, and nobody lay down yet.
Corin had the Ledger out.
Ledger VIII. The green book. Lady Isolde's book, that Lyra had given him in the crypt at Saint Bride's on the night her father died, with the first page written in her mother's brown back-leaning hand and then his own crooked capitals under it. READ THIS FIRST. It was a quarter full already. He opened it at the very back, at the last leaf, where there was nothing written yet. The last leaf he could cut out, later, carefully, with his knife along the stitching, and send south. He took out his pencil.
"What are you doing?" said Lyra.
"The page," said Corin. "For Gideon."
She looked at him. Then she understood. "Now?"
"He's going," said Corin. He did not have to say who. "On the slope, he was so quiet I could hardly hear him. And here it's worse. Here, so close to the Glass..." He stopped. "If I don't do it tonight, I don't think I'll be able to do it at all."
Lyra did not say anything more. She moved round the lamp and sat down close beside him, on his right, where she could see the page. Oren sat back against the north wall of the tent, with his knees up and his sword across them, and took the lamp in his big hand and held it up a little, so that the light fell on the paper.
Corin shut his eyes.
Malakor.
Nothing.
Malakor. The page. Linus's page. For the boy. You said you'd give it to me.
Nothing. Only the hum of the Glass. Only the small hiss of the lamp and the breathing of the other two and, outside, very faint, a goat bell, and the click of bone charms in the dark.
Then, from very far away, a voice.
Boy.
It was so faint. Fainter than it had been on the slope. Like a voice two rooms away, through two shut doors. Like a voice in another house.
Boy. You're very late.
I know. I'm sorry. Can you do it?
A long pause.
I can do it. If you write fast. And if you don't argue with me.
I won't argue.
You always argue. Something like a dry laugh, very far off. Pencil, then.
Corin opened his eyes and put the pencil to the paper.
The putting-back, said Malakor's voice, slowly, one word at a time, with long gaps between them, so that Corin had to wait for each word as you wait for the next drop of water from a leaking roof. For one who has lost a thing. Not burned. Taken. Or given away. Which is the same thing, at the bottom.
Corin wrote. THE PUTTING BACK. FOR ONE WHO HAS LOST A THING. NOT BURNED. TAKEN. OR GIVEN AWAY.
You will need, said Malakor, a thing of your own. A real one. A memory. Not a story you've heard. Not a thing you've read. A thing you were there for. With your own eyes and hands. And it must be a warm one.
YOU WILL NEED A THING OF YOUR OWN. A REAL ONE. A THING YOU WERE THERE FOR. IT MUST BE A WARM ONE.
If it is in a jar, hold the jar in your bare hand until the glass is as warm as your skin. If it is still in you, hold your own hand over your own heart until the hand is warm. Either way. Warm first. Always warm first.
Corin wrote it. His hand was cramping. The pencil was too small for his fingers and the black tips of them made it hard to grip. He wrote it anyway. HOLD THE JAR IN YOUR BARE HAND TILL IT IS WARM.
Then sit with the one you are putting back into. Close. Skin to skin. Your hand on their hand. Or on their face. Somewhere bare. Not through cloth. Never through cloth.
SIT SKIN TO SKIN. NOT THROUGH CLOTH.
The voice stopped. For so long that Corin thought it had gone.
Malakor?
I'm here. Fainter. I'm here, boy. Keep writing. Open the jar, or open your hand. And breathe it toward them. Slowly. The way you'd breathe on a cold window to clear it. Toward their face. Not hard. You are not pushing. You are offering.
OPEN IT. BREATHE IT TOWARD THEM. SLOW. NOT PUSHING. OFFERING.
And while you breathe, say their name. Not their full name. Not the name on the papers. The name you call them. The name you would shout if you saw them across a street.
SAY THEIR NAME. THE NAME YOU CALL THEM.
And then wait. It can take a long while. Sometimes it does not take at all. If it does not take, it was not warm enough, or it was not yours.
Corin wrote. His letters were getting bigger, and more crooked, and further apart, as the lamp shook a little in Oren's hand and the light moved on the page.
Then the voice said, so faint it was hardly there at all:
Tell the boy: quick, and warm, and it has to be something of his own. You can't put back what you don't give.
Corin wrote it. Every word. TELL THE BOY. QUICK AND WARM AND IT HAS TO BE SOMETHING OF HIS OWN. YOU CANT PUT BACK WHAT YOU DONT GIVE.
Then he waited.
Nothing more came.
Malakor?
Nothing.
Is that all of it?
A very long silence. Then, like the last breath of a draft under a door:
That's all of it. That's all there ever was. Linus put three pages round it to make it look clever. And a dry sound, far off, that might have been a laugh. Go to sleep, boy.
And then nothing at all.
Corin sat with the pencil in his hand and the Ledger open on his knee. He found he was breathing hard, as if he had been running. His hand ached from the wrist to the knuckles. The page in front of him was covered, top to bottom, with his big leaning capitals, so crowded at the bottom that the last lines ran into each other.
"Is that it?" said Oren quietly. "Is he done?"
"Yes," said Corin. "He's done."
Oren lowered the lamp. His arm must have been aching too. He had held it up the whole time without a word.
Lyra was looking at the page. Not at Corin. At the page. At the rows of crooked capitals, dark gray on the creamy old paper. And her face had a look on it that Corin had not seen before. A careful look. A reading look.
"Give it here," she said. "I'll read it back to you."
Checking
He gave it to her.
She took the green book in both gloved hands and held it close to the lamp, and Oren lifted the lamp again without being asked, and she bent her head over the page.
She read it slowly. Not because she could not read. She read well, better than Corin did now. But because his letters were hard. He knew they were. They leaned and wobbled and ran into each other. Some of them were too big and some too small. Some of the lines went uphill across the page and some went down. It was the writing of a man who had learned to write once, as a boy, neatly, and then had lost it, and had to learn it again from the beginning, as a grown man, with hands whose fingertips had gone black and could not feel the pencil properly.
She read it aloud. Word by word.
"The putting back. For one who has lost a thing. Not burned. Taken. Or given away."
Her voice was low and careful. The lamp hissed.
"You will need a thing of your own. A real one. A thing you were there for. It must be a warm one."
Corin listened, with his eyes shut, to hear if the words were the same as the words Malakor had said. They were.
"Hold the jar in your bare hand till it is warm." She stopped.
He opened his eyes.
She was looking at the page with a little frown. Her gloved finger had come up. It hovered over the line, and then came down, very gently, onto one word. The tip of the black glove rested on the paper beside one letter.
"That one," she said.
He leaned over to see.
JAR.
Only he had not written JAR. He had written JA and then the last letter backward. The R faced the wrong way, with its round belly on the left side and its leg kicking out to the left, like a letter seen in a mirror.
He stared at it.
He had not seen it. He had looked right at it, writing it, and he had not seen it at all. It had looked right to him. It looked right to him now, almost. If he did not think about it. If he only looked at it the way you look at a face you know, it looked like an R.
But it was not. It was backward.
"It's backward," said Lyra. Not unkindly. Just telling him. "The leg goes the other way."
"Yes," he said. "I see it."
He took the pencil and, very carefully, crossed out the backward letter with a single small line, and wrote a right one above it, small. He had to think about it. He had to think, which way does the belly go? Which way does the leg go? He had to see the shape of it in his head first, before his hand would make it. It came out a little shaky. But it was right.
Lyra watched him do it. Then she went on reading.
"Sit skin to skin. Not through cloth. Open it. Breathe it toward them. Slow. Not pushing. Offering."
She read on. Through the part about the name. Through the part about waiting. She read the long lines at the bottom where his letters had crowded and run together, and twice she had to stop and look hard and say the words over to herself under her breath before she could say them out loud. But she got all of them. She got every one.
And then she stopped again. Her finger came down again.
"That one too," she said.
It was in the last line. In the word DONT. The N. He had written it backward. The slant of the middle stroke went the wrong way, from bottom-left to top-right, so that it looked like a broken ladder.
He had not seen that one either.
He sat and looked at it, and something went through him that he did not have a name for. Not shame, exactly. He did not feel ashamed. It was more like the feeling of putting your foot down on a stair in the dark and finding the stair is not there. Of knowing, all at once and for certain, how much of himself had gone. Not the big things. Not his mother's face, or his own name, or the war. He had known about those. The small things. The things underneath the things. Which way the leg of an R goes. Which way the line of an N slants.
He had not known he had lost those.
And she had found them. Lyra, who could not write a single letter. Who had given her writing away to the fire in a burn, and could never get it back. Who could look at a word and read it, but could not make one. She had sat here by the lamp with her gloved finger and found the two letters he had made wrong, that he could not see.
He fixed the N. He crossed it out and wrote it again, small, above. He had to think about that one too.
"Is that all of them?" he said.
She looked at the page again. All of it. Top to bottom. Slowly. Her lips moving a little.
"Yes," she said. "That's all of them." She gave the book back to him. "The rest are all right. They're ugly. But they're right."
"They lean," said Corin.
"They lean," she said. "It's different." And the corner of her mouth went up.
Oren put the lamp down. He was smiling too, in his beard. Corin could not see it. But he could hear it, in the way Oren breathed out.
"Well," said Oren. "That's the first job the three of us have done together, in all this, that went right the first time."
Corin looked at him.
"Is it?" he said.
And then he heard what he had said. Not, is it? meaning, is that true? But, is it? meaning, I don't know. I don't know what jobs we have done together. I don't remember.
Because he did not. He knew, in the way he knew things from the Ledger, that there had been other times. The cellars under the Bourse. The roof garden. The fire on Midwinter night. He had read about them in his own capitals. But he did not have them. Not the way you have a thing you were there for. They were stories somebody had told him about a man with his name.
This, though. This he had.
The little round tent. The smell of goat fat and goat skin. The lamp in Oren's hand. Lyra's gloved finger on the backward R. This he had been there for. With his own eyes. And he would remember it. He thought he would remember it for a long time.
It was the first thing they had done together that he would.
Lyra was watching his face. He did not know what was on it.
"What?" she said.
"Nothing," he said. Then, because that was not true, and because she always knew when it was not true: "It's the first one I'll remember. The first thing the three of us did. That I'll remember doing."
She did not answer for a moment.
Then she reached out and took the pencil out of his hand, and turned it round in her gloved fingers, and looked at it. As if it were a strange small thing she had found on the ground and did not know the use of.
"Then write that down too," she said, and gave it back to him. "In case."
He turned to the front of the book, to the next clean page after his last entry, and wrote it.
SHE FOUND MY WRONG LETTERS.
He looked at it. The S leaned. The W was too wide. But they were all the right way round. He checked every one.
Lyra checked them too, leaning over his arm. She did not say anything. She only nodded, once, and sat back.
The Price
The door flap moved.
It was Kestrel. She did not come in. She crouched in the opening, with the dark behind her and the cold coming in round her, and looked at the three of them in the lamplight. At the green book open on Corin's knee. At the pencil. At Lyra sitting close by his arm.
"You are not asleep," she said.
"No," said Corin.
She nodded, as if she had expected that. Then she came in. She did it the way the Ashborn seemed to do everything, without fuss, folding her long body down through the low door and sitting on the mat just inside it, with her knees drawn up and her back against the frame. Facing north. Toward the ridge. Toward them.
The lamp shook in the draft and then steadied.
"We have talked," she said. "The old ones and we. About you."
Nobody spoke.
"We will do it," said Kestrel. "Tomorrow night. When the sun is down. We will take the fish girl from you, and the woman who sold children, and all of what you carry of her. Into twelve of us. A little into each. So that you do not walk onto the Glass with her." She looked at Corin steadily. "It is called the rite. We have no other name for it. It is only what we do."
Corin found that his throat had gone tight.
He had not asked for it. He had not even known, until tonight, that such a thing could be done. That a person could take a thing out of you that you had taken, and carry it for you, so that you did not have to. In all his years, in all the Ministry's long rooms and locked racks and silver rods, nobody had ever told him that. Nobody had ever said, you do not have to carry it alone. Nobody had known.
Or nobody had wanted him to know.
"Why?" he said. His voice came out rough. "You don't know me. You don't know any of us."
"No," said Kestrel. "But we know what you are carrying. And we know where you are going with it." She did not look away. "We do not let people drown at our door. Not if we can stop it. Not even strangers."
"And it costs nothing?" said Oren.
He said it quietly, from the back of the tent, with the lamp on the stone beside him and his sword across his knees. He did not say it rudely. He said it the way a soldier asks about a bridge before he marches his men across it. Plainly. Because he needs to know.
Kestrel turned her head and looked at him.
"Everything costs," she said. "You are from the south. You know that better than we do."
"Then what's the price?"
Kestrel was quiet for a moment. Then she turned back to Corin.
"When one of ours dies near you," she said, "you carry a share of them. The way we will carry a share of yours."
The tent was very still.
"That is all," said Kestrel. "It is the same price we all pay. Every one of us. We breathe for each other. We carry each other. If you let twelve of us carry for you tomorrow, then you are one of the ones who carries. While you are here. While you are with us. And if one of us dies near you, on this side of the Glass or on the other, then you will sit with them at the end, and you will breathe, and you will carry your share. Like any of us. Like a child does, when they are old enough." She touched the gray line at the tip of her nose. "That is the price."
Corin looked at her.
He thought of the shelves at the back of his mind. All the people on them. The mages and thieves and murderers and sad old women. Taken. Pulled out. Torn off. Not one of them had ever given him anything. He had never once sat with someone at the end and breathed in what they wanted him to have.
Except Vivienne. And she had not wanted him to have it. She had only wanted it not to go into Remy.
"Is it heavy?" he said. "A share?"
"A share is small," said Kestrel. "A day. A face. A taste. A song. It is not like what you do. It is not a whole person." She paused. "But it is not nothing. You will know them. You will have a little of them in you, until you die. And then someone will breathe it out of you, and carry it on."
He thought about that. About having a little of a stranger in him until he died. A day. A face. A song.
It did not seem like a price at all.
It seemed like the opposite of one.
"Yes," he said.
Kestrel looked at him for a long moment. Then she nodded, once.
"Good," she said.
And from the back of the tent, very low, in a voice like a cart going over cobbles, Oren said, "Saints."
They all looked at him.
He was looking at the roof of the tent, with his head back against the frame, and his eyes shut.
"Another price," said Oren. He opened his eyes and looked at Corin. "That's all this whole thing is, isn't it? Since the start. Since that first night. One price after another. One for the cellars. One for the roof. One for the... the thing on the canal. The shut. You know." He made a gesture with one big hand, a square shape, a gate shape, in the air. "One for every step north. And every time we pay it, there's another one, a bit further on, waiting."
Nobody said anything.
"I'm not saying don't," said Oren. "I'm saying it, that's all. Somebody ought to say it." He shut his eyes again. "Another price. There. I've said it."
Lyra laughed.
It came out of her suddenly, short and surprised, the way laughter comes when you are very tired and have not expected anything to be funny. She put her gloved hand over her mouth at once. But her shoulders were shaking.
And Kestrel, in the doorway, looked at the big gray-bearded soldier with his eyes shut and his sword across his knees, and the corner of her mouth went up again. Further, this time. Nearly all the way.
"This one," she said, "we like."
She got up. She stooped in the door, ready to go out.
"Tomorrow," she said. "After dark. Eat in the day. Sleep in the day, if you can. Do not burn anything. Not one thing. Not even a small one." She looked at Corin. "We need all of you there to do it."
Then she was gone, and the flap fell shut behind her, and the cold that had come in with her slowly went out again.
